# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movies where ABSOLUTELY Nothing happens

**Score:** 176
**Body:** Need movies where literally and figuratively nothing happens. For example:- the entire movie is just a person on a phone call for two hours. A random animal just doing random shit for 2 hours. I know movies like my dinner with andre but i dont want something that has a story or develops meaning and value in the conversation. I need movies that are literally hollow or idle. A conversation movie will only work if the conversation is absolutely pointless

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Empire. The Andy Warhol movie that is just a shot of the Empire State Building. It's eight hours long.
  - That and “Sleep” which is also by Warhol. It’s 5+ hours of watching someone sleep. 
    - I think it was a record of the person who watched the Empire movie.
  - This movie was intended to be projected on a wall and glanced at or briefly looked at as people walk by. There are changes as people in the film go into and come out of the building.  Those who sit and watch it appear to be unaware of the original intent. 
2. It’s possible something is happening in Last Year at Marienbad (1961) but it remains unclear to me. Still it is a very interesting hypnotic viewing experience.

You might like Slacker (1990) as well. Things happen but there is no narrative to speak of.
3. Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975) is what you're looking for. Okay, something happens at the end, but most of it is static shots of her washing dishes or cleaning the bathtub 
  - I also came to recommend this. It's crazy that it's as entertaining as it is when literally nothing happens for almost the entire movie.
4. Coffee And Cigarettes. Just vignettes of people smoking and caffeinating. Somehow still enthralling.
  - Also snapshot of a part of culture that no longer exists.   

Last gasp of the '90s
5. Paint Drying (2016)

## 2. Ghost and the Darkness (1996)

**Score:** 40
**Body:** Hubby and I randomly came across this ‘oldie but goodie’ movie from 1996, Ghostbusters and the Darkness. No spoilers but it stars a young Val Kilner and the coolest young Michael Douglas. Great scenery and character development. Some gore. Not for children.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Who you gonna call?
  - Ghostbusters and the Darkness is the movie mashup we've all been waiting for since the late 90's.
  - Lol
2. A very cool film. The lions are on display at the Field Museum in Chicago
3. Saw it in the cinema. Awesome. True story (as true as 90s movies can make a story). The Ghost and the Darkness really did shred that many. 

Val Kilmer and Michael Douglas make a great team in this and there's plenty of suspense.

If you're looking for something along the same animal lines, Beast, with Idris Elba is modern fun.
4. >Some gore. Not for children.

I very distinctly remember watching this and saying "OK, but **that** was the gore?"  


It's like 5 seconds of gore spread out through the entire movie. This was bordering on PG-13 level; it was all in nanosecond long bites.
  - My now adult daughter who loved horror movies as a kid still can't watch the hospital scene. 
5. And you’re not….🦁
6. This is an all time favorite of mine. I remember my parents rented it back when it first came out. Its a total favorite of mine, I personally love how Vals Irish accent fades pretty quickly after that first train ride lol. All joking aside its a fantastic movie 
7. Michael Douglas is one of the few actors where if I see his name in the cast, I know the movie won't be absolutely terrible. He's made consistently decent movies over the course of a very long career.


## 3. I need more awesome concert films/documentaries. I've listed the ones I've liked below.

**Score:** 20
**Body:** I really enjoyed the following and searching for more...

The Last Waltz, Pink Floyd - Live at Pompeii, Talking Heads - Stop Making Sense, Bittersweet Motel and Grace Jones - One Man Show. Thank you in advance!

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Gimme Shelter
2. Dig! - it's more of a mockumentary featuring two bands: The Brian Jonestown Massacre and The Dandy Warhols.
3. Woodstock (1970)
  - That's actually my next watch! Also, Monterey Pop.
4. Muscle Shoals
5. If you haven't watched the old Mtv Unplugged shows they were great.
6. Shine a Light - The Rolling Stones 
7. Brian Wilson -Smile Live 2004

Ween - Live in Chicago 
  - hell yeah Ween Live in Chicago!
8. You've already listed at least 3 of the best of all time (Last Waltz, Live at Pompeii, Stop Making Sense), and someone else already mentioned Woodstock.  

So here's some that are still really good, if not quite as good as those ones.

Festival Express - documents a 1970 Canadian train tour that featured the Grateful Dead, Janis Joplin, and The Band

Buena Vista Social Club - documentary follows legendary guitarist Ry Cooder and his son as they travel to Cuba and assemble some of the finest musicians in the country.  Started a bit of a Renaissance in interest in Cuban music, and many of the artists featured at the time.  The movie itself has a bit of a "great white saviour" vibe to it that I'm not fond of, but the music is impeccable.

Let it Be - captures the Beatles writing and recording their penultimate album, culminating in an iconic rooftop concert in London.

Monterey Pop - includes sets from the Mamas and the Papas, Simon & Garfunkel, Jefferson Airplane, The Who, Otis Redding, and an iconic performance from Jimi Hendrix.  

Shut Up and Play the Hits - LCD Soundsystem prepares for their biggest concert at Madison Square Garden

Sign 'O' the Times - Prince at his creative and performing peak

and although not an official concert film, there's footage and recordings of Pink Floyd's concert at Ivor Wynne stadium in Hamilton, Ontario in June 1975 that includes the first live performances of material that would eventually become the Animals album.  They're on YouTube, and I highly recommend any Pink Floyd fan should check it out.



## 4. Looking for horror movies with a very specific "southern gothic" or “swamp/backwoods gothic” atmosphere — rural decay, trailer parks, isolation, drugs, fucked-up families, etc.

**Score:** 19
**Body:** I'm looking for horror movies with a really specific aesthetic that I recently realized genuinely creeps me out. I'm not sure if the best term is southern gothic, backwoods gothic, rural gothic or rural-decay horror, but I'll try to describe it.

Think deep rural South / Appalachia / Louisiana bayou type atmosphere. Trailer homes and old shacks in the middle of nowhere, rusting cars and junk in people's yards, swamps or stagnant lagoons nearby, oppressive heat and humidity, mosquitoes, overgrown vegetation, empty roads, drugs/addiction, poverty, weird family dynamics, incest references/generational dysfunction, and neighbors you absolutely would not trust. The biggest thing is the feeling of being far removed from normal society. Like you've accidentally wandered into a tiny community or family that's been isolated for generations and has developed its own rules and ideas about what's normal. Cell service is gone, civilization feels 50 miles away, everybody knows everybody, and if you disappeared there's a genuine feeling that nobody would even know where to start looking.

Sandy Shores/Trevor's home territory in GTA V captures what I mean. That feeling of trailer parks, addicts, guns, family secrets, abandoned buildings and people who've been living in the same forgotten place forever.

I just watched The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974) and the isolated/inbred-family elements were definitely in the right direction, but the age of the movie made it less frightening to me. I'd love something with that basic atmosphere but with modern cinematography, sound design, realistic acting and disturbing imagery that really makes the environment feel believable.

I'm not necessarily looking for a slasher or lots of gore. It can be supernatural, psychological, realistic, indie, foreign, low-budget, whatever. I'm mainly after that deeply uncomfortable feeling of “I should not be here, these people are not operating by the same rules I am, and there is nobody coming to help me.”

Obscure/indie recommendations are especially welcome. What's the best movie you've seen that captures this atmosphere?

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. ‘The skeleton key’
  - This film is fantastic!  OP this is what you want.  Voodoo, swamps, and yes it is Gothic.  Meaning it has elements of the gothic tradition. 
  - Yep This is the first one that popped into my head. And not just because I worked on it. I lived right near the Laundromat/ "VooDoo store" in the movie on the west bank of New Orleans, Algiers Point.
2. The first season of true detective is similar to what you’re looking for if you want a psychological thriller. 
  - Also Sharp Objects
3. The Gift - early Cate Blanchett film. 
4. Night of the Hunter is not, strictly speaking, horror. But it's a stone cold classic, and it scares me.
5. Jug face
6. Deliverance   
Nothing but Trouble  
American Horror Story: Coven tv series 
7. Southern Comfort

## 5. Non true crime documentary recommendations

**Score:** 17
**Body:** I'm looking for for documentaries that are NOT true crime/murder/suicide/too much SA. I've watched a lot on those topics and need a moral break right now. 

  
Im in the US and currently have Netflix, hulu, prime and most channels that public libraries offer. I can possibly get access to HBO and YouTube TV. So any recommendations available for streaming on those would be greatly appreciated!

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Man on a Wire, Three Identical Strangers (fascjnating but a little sad)   
One of my favorites is Searching for Sugarman about an OBSCURE American singer whose music becomes incredibly important in South Africa during the apartheid. Two South Africans decades later go in search of the singer. It is a wild wild ride. Won best picture. And the music is great
  - Searching for Sugarman was incredible 
  - yes to 3 identical strangers. very disturbing
2. Touching The Void.
3. Grizzly Man. Anything by Werner Herzog, really 
4. The Rescue

20 Feet from Stardom
5. The King of Kong
6. Slight off the target, but two faux documentary series, both on Netflix I think. 

Cunk on Earth  
The tone is like a British historical documentary, but the host is so clueless it’s hilarious.  And they interview real experts who have to answer ridiculous questions.  

Documentary Now!   
A series that mocks different types of documentaries.  Cult leader, 70s band, musical behind the scenes, artist profile, unique chef. All are very funny. 

Great brain cleansers. 
7. A few of my favourites:

Jiro Dreams of Sushi

Searching for Sugar Man

Mr Scorsese

Hoop Dreams

The Last Dance
8. Tom Hiddleston does Pompeii is easy on the eyes.

## 3. What are the most WTF tonal shifts you've seen in a movie? Especially if its lighthearted but goes from zero to one hundred right away.

## 5. I loved Tenet

**Score:** 163
**Body:** Just like what Prometheus is to the Alien Franchise to me, Tenet is to Christopher Nolan's filmography to me. A divisive movie part of something loved that I never expected to actually enjoyed... People described that this movie describes the best and worst of Christopher's direction... I'm mixed on that, but I can't explain it... It's too complicated for me to describe... I still liked the movie though!

Judging by the movie's description on Letterboxd, the concept of using the direction of time (As Christopher Nolan described it) to stop World War 3 is nuts and hilarious... Yet, it actually works for me. That part where John David Washington's fighting a random masked guy was hilarious but I couldn't stop to enjoy this movie because I was really interested into the plot of this movie. The action's structure is honestly genius but also very confusing... The parts where they reveal on the latter half that they're actually part of the first half is really cool, but also... How did this kind of logic happened? Where did it come from? But I feel like that on rewatch or thinking about it, this movie might be better or atleast make a little more sense to me... Performances are great as always, and the visuals are amazing as always... People are divided on the music, but I did get used to it as the movie goes on. Wasn't really digged into Kat's subplot that much, and some of the action can get confusing like I said... But happily, consider me a Tenet enjoyer!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Homerist Olga Levaniouk, who has written extensively about Penelope, gives her take on Nolan's version of the character.

**Score:** 43
**Body:** [https://continuum.fas.harvard.edu/initial-thoughts-on-penelope-in-nolans-odyssey/](https://continuum.fas.harvard.edu/initial-thoughts-on-penelope-in-nolans-odyssey/)

Olga Levaniouk has become the latest classicist to enter the foray over Christopher Nolan's adaption of the Odyssey. She gives her opinion on the film generally, before moving on to her area of expertise in Penelope.

To sum her thoughts, while she wishes some scenes from the poem made the cut into the film ("the test of the bed"), and describes the woman in the poem as more complex, she is overall impressed with how the screenplay & Anne Hathaway's performance developed her characterization, despite the limited screen time. And goes as far as to call this her favourite version of the character outside the original poem.

What are your thoughts on this review, and on Nolan's Penelope broadly?

Critics have described Hathaway's performance as a highlight of the film (I concur), and I think Levaniouk makes some very compelling points about how the broader film & screenplay serves her, given the economic screentime that is available for the character. Even though — as Levaniouk acknowledges —  some degree of truncation was inevitable in the process of cinematic adaptation.

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I think this is a well considered review underlining that it’s wise to moderate expectations on how well a Hollywood blockbuster will might adapt a complex literary work. And that it’s worth applauding what the movie achieves within the frame it sets for itself. 
  - The film's job isn't to give us everything that's in the book. It's not even to give us most of the things that are in the book. The film's job is to say what it wants to say using the book as a jumping-off point.

I hate - HATE - "faithful" adaptations. There is nothing more boring than a movie that just follows the book, scene by scene, beat by beat, same tone, same themes, just making it so you can "see it on the screen." Harry Potter, LOTR, Sin City, it doesn't matter. If I want to "see" the book I'll read the book and use my imagination. These movies feel to me like they exist only to cash in on successful IP, not add to the great global conversation we are having through art.

Give me The Shining (give me literally anything Kubrick adapted), give me Minority Report or O Brother Where Art Thou, Starship Troopers, Kurosawa's Ran, give me the adaptations that take the material to a new place and sit in conversation with it, offering their own insights and ideas and vision. I may not like the vision or concur with the thesis of the film, but I at least respect that they took a swing.

Say what you will about Nolan's Odyssey (and I do have quite a few critiques), at least it has something to say that belongs to the film and the film alone. Missing scenes from the book do not bother it, nor do they bother me.
    - As someone with aphantasia (no visual imagination) I have to say I do appreciate seeing worlds fleshed out for the first time. LOTR also made thoughtful changes to adapt the leisurely prose to the silver screen, more successfully than Nolan’s Odyssey. But I agree that scene for scene adaptations tend to feel somewhat manufactured - and box in the story and themes
  - What a lot of people are missing is the difficulty in fitting that much story into one movie. Some of the most highly regarded adaptations of books cut a ton of content in order to fit them in a movie and never got the same amount of criticism. LOTR cut a ton of important scenes such as the journey out of the Shire/Tom Bombadil/Saruman taking over the Shire. Dune completely changes the whole tone from a dialogue heavy narrative to a more visual showcase with minimal dialogue. There were moments in The Odyssey that seemed rushed and many cut scenes but I think it was just a requirement to finish in time. The adaptation has to become its own story and I think Nolan did an amazing job with the limitations he had to consider.
2. Fascinating article, & I was also impressed with how much was expressed with body language & gesture over words, with reflects how a queen in this situation would express herself. What was new to me is how the film compared Penelope to the Trojans: she too has been under siege, & living in her kingdom’s ruins. Odysseus makes amends in part by freeing her from it, & acceding to her original wishes to leave it behind.
3. I just saw the movie last night. I've read both Wilson pieces (much of which I just straight disagree with, some of it I at least see her point), along with [another wonderful piece](https://talesoftimesforgotten.com/2026/07/23/an-ancient-historians-breakdown-of-christopher-nolans-the-odyssey/) from another classics prof just breaking down some of the context and changes between the movie and the text, and now this.

But by far the wisest simplest thing anyone has said about this movie is someone on Bluesky I can't find right now, they said ***this movie is more of a remix than a cover***\*\*.\*\*

Nolan is using The Odyssey (book) as a lens through which to think of a lot of different ideas about Empire, greatness, collapse, much of it more about today than about the past. He's using the text for what it is - source material - and framing what he really wants to say and explore through it. As the author of the article says, "Nolan’s *Odyssey* strikes me not so much as an adaptation but as a fascinating dialogue with Homer." All these things, whether they are films, new translations, they are all in dialogue not only with Homer but with each other. It's all a conversation using this text as a starting point.

So I don't really care much about how much is truncated or left out of the text, or what new stuff is put in. At the point that I accept that this new film is not about the same things the poem is about, I only care about how the film actually achieves what it wants to say. I don't need this Penelope to be like the original Penelope. In fact, what I like about this movie is how it subverts our understandings of what we think O&P ought to be like.

In Penelope, we get less of the loyal and wise long-suffering wife and more of a smart and truly cunning stateswoman, who has been holding everything together without any credit, running the entire kingdom, who sets up the final battle completely silently or in code and is always one step ahead of the rest of the story, even her son. In many ways she is the real Odysseus here.

As for Odysseus, I defer to this excellent article on [rogerebert.com](http://rogerebert.com) that reflects a lot of my thoughts on the movie's themes and ideas - [https://www.rogerebert.com/features/the-people-from-the-sea-how-the-odyssey-is-about-america](https://www.rogerebert.com/features/the-people-from-the-sea-how-the-odyssey-is-about-america)

I agree Anne Hathaway is fantastic in this movie. Quiet intensity, rage, tenderness, and all while not embodying the "theatre kid" vibes she had when she was younger. She has grown into a truly marvelous actor (she was already good before, but had so much theatre kid energy that got in the way of her work), and has quietly built a really interesting and selective filmography over the last 5 years or so. She was stunning in *Eileen* which was otherwise very flawed, for example.
  - Probably this tweet: https://x.com/BretDevereaux/status/2078972264205205772 by Bret Devereaux crossposted to blue sky

## 2. The way in which audiences view film adaptations is fundamentally broken

**Score:** 35
**Body:** When it comes to criticising adaptations of IP and literature, I’ve noticed something: when assessing the quality of a movie, there is an expectation for the film to function as the definitive interpretation and version of the original work. It often feels like audiences are holding a score card, and assessing how well the adaptation succeeds in fulfilling all of the metrics on the accuracy score card.

To illustrate this point, I’m going to use a movie I consider bad: Man of Steel. If I were to explain why I hate this movie, I would talk about its terrible misuse of non-linear storytelling, it’s failure to connect us with its lead character and the poorly developed romance. Yet, in spite of all of my problems with the movie, I’ve never had an issue with the aspect of it that I often see most criticised: the fact that Jonathan Kent tells him that perhaps he should’ve let those kids die.

Yes, it is a big diversion from the source material, but I do not understand the need to view every adaptation as if should be - or is even *aspiring* to me - the definitive interpretation of a story. Stories exist to be retold, and each interpretation is simply one singular artist’s reimagining of the source material. 

I see this same line of thinking when it comes to Tom Holland’s Spider-Man: Homecoming trilogy. There is plenty to criticise in those movies - the flat cinematography, the indistinct directing. These are fair criticisms, because they concern the quality of the movie and how it functions as a piece of storytelling. But I don’t understand the criticisms that ‘Spider-Man’s villains should not be connected to Tony Stark’ or that ‘Spider-Man shouldn’t be using technology. To me, that’s as nonsensical as reading Absolute Batman and coming away thinking “this is a bad adaptation, because Batman should be rich, not blue collar.”

If you want a version of The Odyssey with the No Man pun, that exists. If you want a version of Spider-Man where he does not use technology, that exists too. I do not understand - and do not agree with the notion - that an adaptation exists to fulfill the purpose of a perfect adaptation. Each adaptation should be treated like a distinct vision of an artist. 

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Though I do somewhat agree with the point this feels like it strangely assumes there are an infinite number of adaptations for every source material, when the reality is that most works, especially non-classic ones, are very rarely going to get more than one, certainly no more than one high budget hollywood adaptation, so I don’t think it’s unfair to dread an adaptation that abandons the source material if it may be the only one you’re liable to get.

Idk I think people are too defensive about their adaptations, if you’re going to work off a source material then you should expect it to be viewed in the context of the material you’re basing it off, if you can’t face criticism to that effect then you should probably be making your own thing.

Edit: to elaborate a little people keep going off about juvenile critics around this film but just as pervasive a discourse seems to be this strange defensiveness over it, as if every criticism is an assault against their identity. Emily Wilson is getting dragged over a critique that is largely tame, she even praises the film as entertainment less than an adaptation and yet fans seem driven into an absolute frenzy over it.
  - Right. Adapting the Odyssey or Shakespeare literally would be pointless; it's been done. Meanwhile, they're so widely known that they make a good framework to add your own ideas, because the conversation with our shared cultural heritage is interesting and makes reinterpreted adaptations stronger than they could be on their own.

None of that applies to the 90+% of adaptations that aren't universal cultural touchstones. If you adapt other media to film, you are starting from a blueprint that already succeeded as a story. Someone did the work for you. You can take what they already had, or you can risk redoing that work yourself to make changes. That's a fundamentally arrogant choice, and while it can work, it usually doesn't.

For a recent example, look at Supergirl. It was already a story in a visual medium, so the adaptation work could've been very direct, using the designs, color palette, themes, and characters of the original story. Even the shots, if they'd wanted.

Instead, Ana Nogueira and Craig Gillespie decided they could do it better from scratch. Unfortunately, they didn't understand why the original work had the plot beats and designs that it did or how those slowly reinforced each other and built up the conclusion. When they made changes, they broke the parts that made the story work. The movie sucked, and it failed critically and financially.

Craig Gillespie isn't even a terrible director! One of the risks of adaptations that people miss is that even if you can make a good movie on your own, that does *not* mean you can make a successful adaptation, because you're being handed a story that was built with someone else's tools, and functions in ways you don't use yourself and might not be good at. This also comes up in Supergirl with the way Gillespie tries to use Gunn's directing style instead of his own, and falls on his face there too.

If they had done a direct adaptation, their lacking creative abilities wouldn't have mattered as much. They could've stuck to executing mechanically, and gotten a better result.

About the adaptation problem, besides what others people pointed out (one adaptation displaces others, so obviously people who feel like they missed out may be bitter about it), there's for me the question of, *why* did this need to be an adaptation? You can make original stories. You can also make overt parodies or deconstructions if your goal is to do some kind of meta-commentary on existing and well-known works; anyone can tell what Galaxy Quest and Watchmen are about, even though they're not explicitly mentioning Star Trek or the DC universe superheroes. There are many Superman expys out there, some played straight, many subversive (Omni-man, Homelander), and none of them are an issue because they're just that, expys, original characters who take the basis of that known one and spin it in a completely different direction, often to make a metatextual point.

The issue is, if you announce you're adapting X (and in the case of modern works, buy the rights to X), at what level of difference from the actual source material does your movie stop being anything you could call an adaptation and becomes merely an original story using the supposed source material for its brand recognition value? One is an artistically respectable enterprise, and the other is intellectually bankrupt. The line is blurry but it exists, and it makes sense that people complain about this sometimes.

Finally, honestly, I believe in practice a movie being good absolves almost all sins, and a movie being bad makes them stand out more. If your bold adaptation choices end up producing a good result, almost no one cares. In fact in comics there's several instances where adaptational choices *flowed back* in the original comics, because they were so good they just became the new canon in people's minds. But if the result is poor, then everyone will nitpick it to hell in an attempt to analyse and find out *what* precisely went wrong, and inevitably the adaptational choices end up under scrutiny too. If something wasn't broken to begin with and now it is, the misguided attempts to fix it are certainly a potential cause.

When Auggie walks away, I don't see it as taking the moral high ground; it feels like she is giving up her influence over future difficult decisions. Leaving doesn't make humanity more ethical; it just means one of the smartest people is no longer advocating for better choices.

Imagine a train heading toward eight billion people. The first measure to slow it down costs 1,000 lives, horrific, yet necessary. After that, more decisions must be made, and sacrifices may still be required. One engineer witnesses the sacrifice and walks away, but another stays, knowing that leaving means losing the chance to influence what happens next. That's how I view Auggie.

My criticism is not that she should have been more ruthless, but that she confuses keeping her conscience clean with fulfilling her responsibility. True moral courage is staying in the room long enough to make the next decision less terrible.

In contrast, I found Jin’s arc more compelling. She is emotionally aware of the costs of her choices and understands that walking away doesn’t stop history; it just silences her voice.

## 5. The Odyssey: does what it's trying to do well

**Score:** 0
**Body:** 4/5

When approaching mythology or folklore, there's two approaches: the realist and the sociological. For example The Craft (1996) takes a realist approach to witchcraft: powers are real, we see the effect they have on their wielders and those around them. The Witch (2015), and films around the Salem Witch Trials, are sociological. They explore the attitudes that led people to fear witches and burn women at the stake. Likewise with vampires, there's countless realist vampire films but Carmilla (2019) takes a sociological approach: showing how a girl is believed to be the devil and staked by a tent peg.

Nolan's Odyssey, in my understanding, takes a sociological approach. Its haters are missing the point that it's not trying to be a picture book illustration of scenes from the poem. It's trying to portray what kind of things might have happened around 1000 BC, a few centuries before Homer, that led to the stories of witches turning men to pigs, of Zeus and Athena on Olympus, of Sirens leading men to rocks.

So while it's true that for example Athena in the poem takes an active role, pleading with Zeus to be allowed to free Odysseus, here Athena is a projection of Odysseus's guilt and trauma of the war. We see her as one of the Trojan girls killed (and presumably many were raped, although this isn't shown) and that haunts Odysseus.

And therefore the casting is fairly color-blind and the language contemporary American, because he's not trying to be totally faithful to the poem but imagine the loss of xenia - the brutality of the Trojan War and how that ripped apart society. Helen becomes an abused wife, Zeus' Law that men should be good to women is broken and that's going to lead to civilizational collapse.

Where I don't give it 5\* is due to some clunkiness in explaining this, "our age of bronze is collapsing" etc are rather too on the nose for it to be a masterpiece (something Nolan has been pulled up for elsewhere, such as in Interstellar).

But with the discourse around this film, if you see it not as an attempted dramatization of The Odyssey but as an exploration of what might have happened to create the stories that became The Odyssey, it's powerful and effective.
